learn.title: Putting values into text
learn.body: To print a variable you put a placeholder in the text, then give the value after a comma. The placeholder is a format specifier. It starts with `%` and a letter that says what kind of value goes there.

learn.title: The common ones
learn.body: `%d` or `%i` is an int. `%c` is a char. `%f` is a float or double. `%s` is text. `%%` prints a percent sign. `%zu` prints a size. The type of the value must match the specifier, or the output is wrong.

learn.title: Controlling the look
Reading input with scanf
learn.body: `scanf` reads what the user types. It uses the same specifiers, and you pass the variable's address with `&`. For an int use `%d`. For a double use `%lf`. For printing, `%f` works for both.

learn.title: Reading a number
learn.body: Here the user typed 21. The prompt and the answer appear together.

learn.title: Reading the scanf line
steps: `%d` says to read a whole number
`&n` gives scanf the place in memory to put it
After the user types 21 and Enter, `n` holds 21

learn.body: Do not forget the `&` in scanf. Leaving it out is a bug that compilers only sometimes warn about.

questions.prompt: `printf("[%5d]", 42);` prints brackets around a number padded to width 5. How many spaces are before 42? Type the number.
questions.explanation: Width 5 means five characters in total. `42` is two, so three spaces pad the left.
